chapter.title: Resume, mocks and final review
chapter.summary: Resume evidence and company targeting, then the March mock loops, full simulations and the final review.

lessons.title: Resume evidence and company targeting
lessons.summary: Make every resume claim defensible, tailor the top third per role, build a target tracker, and prepare recruiter and hiring-manager answers.
keyPoints: A resume is a list of claims you must defend line by line; every claim needs evidence you can open.
Edit the positioning statement so each noun is true; do not claim production experience you lack.
Strong bullets state action, scope and a measured result; use numbers only if you can name the measurement.
Tailor the top third (title, positioning, skills, first bullets) per role family, using the job description's vocabulary only where honest.
The weakest-part column of your claims table is your prepared answer to which claim is weakest.
A project README with evaluation, failure analysis and limits separates your work from a tutorial clone.
ATS basics: one column, standard headings, selectable text, no keyword stuffing.
A tracker with requirements, gaps, fit, referral, stage and a dated next action turns the search into a managed pipeline.

check.q: Your resume bullet says 'Improved accuracy by 40%' but you can't name the dataset or measurement. What should you do?
options: Keep it; interviewers rarely ask
Increase it so it stands out
Move it into the skills section
Remove the number or replace it with a sourced result and describe scope and verification honestly
check.why: An unsourced number collapses under follow-up questions and damages credibility. Either find the measurement or describe the scope and verification without inventing a metric.

check.q: What is the main purpose of the 'weakest part' column in a claims-to-evidence table?
options: To list claims to delete from the resume
To prepare an honest answer to 'which claim is weakest?' and to direct what you study next
To satisfy ATS keyword matching
To compare yourself with other candidates
check.why: It forces you to find the edge of each claim before an interviewer does, gives you a prepared honest answer, and turns the edge into a study or build task.

check.q: A job description lists Kubernetes, which you have never used. What is the right move on your tailored resume?
options: Add Kubernetes to the skills list to pass the filter
Replace it with Docker without comment
Don't claim it; record it as a gap, and either learn and build something small or be upfront about it
List it under projects with the word 'familiar'
check.why: Claims you cannot defend get probed and cost you credibility. Treat the gap as a plan item (learn, build, or leave it off) and be honest in conversation.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
> **Outcome:** Resume evidence, job matching, project README, role-specific preparation.
> **Prerequisites:** At least one project built.
> **Estimated time:** 45 min reading, then the hands-on task. Produce: Resume v1 + target company tracker.

## What this week is for

Your resume is not a biography; it is **a list of claims you will be asked to defend line by line**. In a GenAI interview loop the first screens (recruiter, hiring manager) test whether your claims are specific, true and relevant to the role, and later rounds open each claim like a ticket: "what exactly did you do, how do you know it worked, what broke?". This week you make the resume defensible, aim it at specific roles, and build the tracker that turns a vague job hunt into a managed pipeline. The same days also keep your technical skills warm (Python, SQL, LLM fundamentals, RAG), which is what the March 1-7 schedule in the Week plan does.

The honesty rule is non-negotiable and also strategically sound: **never claim experience you lack**. Interviewers probe claims until they find the edge of your knowledge. An honest "I built this as a project, not in production" survives that probing; an inflated claim collapses on the third follow-up and takes your credibility with it.

## Step 1: positioning statement

A positioning statement is two lines at the top of the resume that say who you are and what you want. A starting template, to be **edited to match your actual experience**:

> Software engineer with experience building backend systems and APIs, expanding into AI-powered applications with Python, LLM integration, retrieval-augmented generation, agent workflows, evaluation and production deployment.

Edit it so every noun is true. If you have not deployed an LLM service to real users, change "production deployment" to "deployment practices (Docker, CI, monitoring) demonstrated in projects". If you have not built agents, drop "agent workflows" until you have a project that demonstrates it. Then **tailor the top third** of the page per job description: the title line, positioning statement, skills block and the first two bullets are what a recruiter reads in the first ten seconds, so those are the parts you reorder to match each role family (AI application engineer, GenAI backend, agentic systems, ML platform).

## Step 2: map every claim to evidence

Build a table before you write a single bullet. Every claim gets a row; a row without evidence is cut or rewritten.

| Claim | Evidence you can open | Who or what confirms it | Weakest part | Interview-safe wording |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Built a RAG search over internal docs | Repo path, README, eval notebook | Eval results, a colleague who used it | No online user feedback yet | "Built and evaluated a RAG prototype on 2,000 docs" |
| Reduced API p95 latency | Pull request, dashboard screenshot | Teammate on the team | Measured on one endpoint | "Cut p95 on the order lookup endpoint from X to Y (load test)" |
| Python | Repos, code review | Public repos | Async depth | List it, expect a coding round |

The **weakest part** column is the most important one. It is your answer to the guaranteed question "which claim is weakest?" and it tells you what to study before the interview.

## Step 3: write bullets with action, scope, result

A strong bullet has **action** (what you personally did, past tense verb), **scope** (system, scale or constraint) and **result** (what changed), where the result carries a number **only if you measured it**.

| Weak | Why | Stronger (template, fill with your facts) |
|---|---|---|
| Responsible for improving search | Duty, not action; no scope or result | Built hybrid keyword and vector retrieval for a document search feature over N documents; evaluated on M labelled queries |
| Worked on AI chatbot in production | "Worked on" hides your role; "production" unproven | Implemented the retrieval and prompt layer of a support chatbot (FastAPI, PostgreSQL); added an eval set and CI check |
| Improved accuracy by 40% | Unsourced number | Raised answer-correctness on a 60-question eval set from X to Y by adding reranking (notebook linked in README) |

Rules: one idea per bullet, under about 30 words, start with a strong verb, name technologies where they were genuinely used, never write a number you cannot source, say "prototype", "project" or "internal tool" when that is what it was. If there is no measurable result, describe the scope and the verification honestly ("covered by 40 unit tests and an offline eval") rather than inventing a percentage. Never use "we" as the subject; say what you did.

## Step 4: project README that supports the resume

A recruiter or engineer opens your repository for two minutes. Structure:

```text
# Project name: one-line purpose
## Problem and users          what it solves, who for, what it does not do
## Demo                       screenshot, short video or live link
## Architecture               one diagram, 5-8 boxes, data flow
## Key decisions              3 bullets: choice, alternative rejected, why
## Evaluation                 dataset size, metrics, results, honest limits
## Run it                     3 commands to run locally, tests, env vars
## Failure analysis           one real bug or failure, root cause, fix
## Limitations and next steps what is not production-ready
```

Evaluation and failure analysis are what separate your project from a tutorial clone. State the dataset size and how labels were created. Do not paste benchmark numbers you did not run.

## Step 5: ATS basics

An applicant tracking system parses your file into fields so recruiters can search it. Practical rules: one column; standard headings (Experience, Projects, Skills, Education); a text-selectable PDF or DOCX (not an image); no key information inside tables, text boxes or icons; consistent date format; the job title and technologies written the way the job description writes them **when true** (for example "PostgreSQL", not only "Postgres", if the JD uses it). Do not keyword-stuff or hide white text; humans read it afterwards and it reads as dishonest. Treat "ATS score" tools as rough linters, not truth.

## Step 6: choose targets and track them

Pick 3 to 4 **role families** and write for each a one-paragraph profile: the requirements that repeat in job descriptions, and which of your projects and bullets evidence them. Then build a pipeline of 20 to 30 companies in tiers (reach, target, safe). For each company record the tracker fields: company, role family, JD requirements, evidence match and gaps, fit score 1 to 5, referral, stage, next action with date.

| Field | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| JD requirements (top 6 to 8) | Drives the tailored top third and your study plan |
| Evidence match and gaps | Honest view of fit; gaps become study or build tasks, or are simply not claimed |
| Fit (1-5) | Prioritises effort: apply and prepare deeply for 4 and 5 |
| Referral | Referrals typically get read sooner; track name, relationship, status |
| Stage and next action with date | Prevents silent stalls; review weekly |

**Outreach basics:** a referral request or a message to a recruiter is short (under 100 words), specific (role link, why you fit in two lines with one piece of evidence), easy to act on (attach resume, offer to send a project link), and polite about no response. Follow up once after about a week. Never mass-spam; never exaggerate in a message.

## Common failure modes

Duties instead of achievements; unsourced numbers; "production" claims you cannot defend; a skills list of 40 technologies you cannot discuss; one generic resume for every role; a tracker you stop updating; applying before the project README and eval exist; pretending a tutorial project is original work.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. The resume listed 'LangChain, LlamaIndex, RAG, agents, fine-tuning' for a weekend clone. The README was the framework's README. Target companies were a list of logos with no JD decode and no person to write to. A bullet said 'reduced latency 50%' with no before/after or workload. In the screen they could not map each claim to a file or a metric. They applied to scientist roles with no maths story.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer: 'This bullet says you built a production RAG. What is in production?' Outline: who uses it, the eval that gates a release, the on-call path, and what is still a prototype. Follow-up: 'Why this company?' Answer: one product constraint from their JD (permissions, cost, language) and how your artifact speaks to it.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut the tool salad, the unofficial title, and any number you cannot source. Keep three evidence-backed bullets, a README that is yours, and a tracker of companies with a decoded JD.

parts.label: Worked example
parts.body:
## Goal and artifact

Artifact: **resume v1 plus a target company tracker**. The code gives you two small tools that make the process repeatable: a bullet linter that enforces the evidence rule, and a tracker schema with the queries you run in the Sunday review. Run `python resume_audit.py` to see the checks pass; then use the functions on your own bullets.

## How to use the tools

1. Create a list of dictionaries, one per bullet, with `text`, `evidence` and, when the text contains a number, `metric_source`.
2. Run `audit_bullet` on each. A non-empty result is a to-do item, not an insult. The linter checks: a strong past-tense opening, length, evidence present, numbers have a source, risky claims ("production", "at scale", "expert", "architected") have evidence, and "we" does not replace "I".
3. Use `coverage` against the requirements you copy from a job description. It reports covered requirements and **gaps**. Gaps are honest output: study them, build a small project that evidences them, or leave them off the resume.
4. Load `tracker.sql` into SQLite (`sqlite3 targets.db < tracker.sql`), insert your companies, and run the two queries every Sunday.

## What the linter cannot do

It cannot tell whether a bullet is true or impressive. It only enforces that every claim has a place you can point to. A bullet that passes can still be dull; a bullet that fails is a risk. Treat it as a gate before you show the resume to anyone.

## Example: before and after (illustrative, replace with your facts)

| Before | Problem | After |
|---|---|---|
| Worked on an AI assistant at scale in production | Vague role, unprovable scale and production | Implemented the retrieval layer (PostgreSQL full-text search plus embeddings) for an internal documentation assistant used by one team; added an offline eval of 50 questions to CI |
| Improved performance by 60% | No scope, no source | Reduced p95 latency of the order lookup endpoint from 800 ms to 300 ms by adding a composite index and a query rewrite; measured with a k6 load test |
| Built RAG pipeline | No evidence or outcome | Built a RAG prototype over 2,000 policy documents (chunking, hybrid search, citations); evaluated on 40 labelled questions, README documents the failures |

The after rows contain illustrative numbers. Use a number only if you can name the measurement behind it; otherwise describe scope and verification instead.

## The tailoring routine (30 minutes per application)

1. Copy the job description's top 6 to 8 requirements into the tracker row.
2. Mark each requirement: covered (cite the bullet), partially (cite a project), gap.
3. Reorder the top third: title line, positioning statement, skills block, first two bullets, so the covered requirements appear first and in the JD's vocabulary where honest.
4. Do not add anything from the gap list. If a gap is critical and you have two weeks, add a task to your study plan and apply later or be upfront in the conversation.
5. Save the tailored PDF with a clear name and record the version in the tracker.

## Outreach message skeleton

```text
Subject: AI application engineer role: [one line of evidence]

Hi [name],
I'm a backend engineer with [X years] building APIs in [stack]. I saw the [role] opening
and built [project] that does [one specific thing] (repo: [link]); it covers [requirement 1]
and [requirement 2] from the posting.
Would you be open to a quick chat or a referral? Resume attached. Thanks for your time,
[name]
```

Keep it under 100 words, include one verifiable link, and send a single follow-up after about a week.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. The resume listed 'LangChain, LlamaIndex, RAG, agents, fine-tuning' for a weekend clone. The README was the framework's README. Target companies were a list of logos with no JD decode and no person to write to. A bullet said 'reduced latency 50%' with no before/after or workload. In the screen they could not map each claim to a file or a metric. They applied to scientist roles with no maths story.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'This bullet says you built a production RAG. What is in production?' Outline: who uses it, the eval that gates a release, the on-call path, and what is still a prototype. Follow-up: 'Why this company?' Answer: one product constraint from their JD (permissions, cost, language) and how your artifact speaks to it.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut the tool salad, the unofficial title, and any number you cannot source. Keep three evidence-backed bullets, a README that is yours, and a tracker of companies with a decoded JD.

code.source:
-- Target company tracker. SQLite or Postgres. Keep it boring and current.
CREATE TABLE targets (
  id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  company       TEXT NOT NULL,
  role_title    TEXT NOT NULL,
  role_family   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (role_family IN ('ai_app_engineer','genai_backend','agentic_engineer','ml_platform','other')),
  jd_url        TEXT,
  jd_requirements TEXT,                 -- top 6 to 8 requirements copied from the JD
  evidence_match  TEXT,                 -- which of your projects or bullets cover which requirement
  gaps          TEXT,                   -- honest gaps and the plan: learn, build, or do not claim
  fit           INTEGER CHECK (fit BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  referral      TEXT,                   -- name and status, or 'none'
  stage         TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'researching'
                CHECK (stage IN ('researching','tailoring','applied','recruiter_screen','technical','onsite','offer','closed')),
  next_action   TEXT,
  next_action_on DATE,
  updated_on    DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

-- What needs attention this week
SELECT company, role_title, stage, next_action, next_action_on
FROM targets
WHERE stage NOT IN ('offer', 'closed')
  AND (next_action_on IS NULL OR next_action_on <= CURRENT_DATE + 7)
ORDER BY fit DESC, next_action_on;

-- Stale rows: no update for 10 days
SELECT company, role_title, stage, updated_on
FROM targets
WHERE stage NOT IN ('offer', 'closed') AND updated_on < CURRENT_DATE - 10;

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
The recruiter and hiring-manager screens are conversational but graded. They check specificity, ownership, honesty and motivation. Prepare spoken answers in the structure below, using your real facts. Where this lesson shows a fictional detail, it is a template: replace it or delete it.

## Q1. What was your contribution to this project?

**Define.** Your contribution is the specific part you personally designed, built or decided, separate from what the team did.

**Mechanism.** State the project's goal in one sentence, then split: "the team did A; I owned B". Name two concrete things you did (a component, a decision, a fix) and how you know it worked (test, metric, user feedback). Use "I" for your actions and "we" only for genuinely shared work.

**Decision.** If the answer is "I did most of it", say so with evidence. If your part was small, say that and describe what you learned from the rest.

**Trade-off.** Claiming too much invites probing you cannot survive; claiming too little undersells you. Calibrate to what you can show.

**Evidence.** A pull request, design doc, README section or dashboard you can name. If it is a personal project, point at the repository and commit history.

**Failure mode to mention.** Saying "we" for everything, so the interviewer cannot tell what you did.

**60-90 second version:** "The project was [one-line goal]. The team built [A]. I owned [B]: specifically I designed [thing] and implemented [thing]. For example, I [concrete decision] because [reason], and I verified it with [test or measurement]. The part I did not own was [C], so I can discuss it at a higher level."

**Follow-ups.**
- *What was the hardest bug?* Pick one with symptom, root cause, fix and prevention.
- *What would you change?* One specific design change with the reason.
- *Who can confirm this?* Name a real colleague or artifact.

## Q2. Which claim on your resume is weakest?

**Define.** The weakest claim is the one with the least evidence or the shallowest understanding. Naming it yourself shows self-awareness.

**Mechanism.** From your claims-to-evidence table, pick the row whose "weakest part" is real. Say what is solid, what is not, and what you have done to close the gap.

**Decision.** Choose a claim that is genuinely weaker but not central to the role. Do not name a fake weakness.

**Trade-off.** Candour costs a little in the moment and buys credibility for every other claim.

**Evidence.** The plan you already started: a project, a study log, a test you ran.

**Failure mode to mention.** Having no answer, or choosing a "weakness" that is a disguised strength.

**60-90 second version:** "The weakest is probably [claim]. I [did X, which is real], but I have not [Y, for example run it under production load / operated it on call]. To close that, I [did something concrete], and I'm clear in interviews that this is project experience. The claims I'm most confident in are [A and B] because [evidence]."

**Follow-ups.** *How would you get production experience?* Name realistic steps: deploy with monitoring, load test, run an on-call style drill, contribute to an open-source project. *Does this disqualify you?* Explain which of the role's needs you cover today.

## Q3. Why do you want to leave your current role?

**Define.** A forward-looking explanation of what you want next, stated without blaming your employer.

**Mechanism.** Two parts: what you have learned and valued, and what you want more of that the next role provides (more AI work, more ownership, larger scale). Tie it to the specific role.

**Decision.** Never criticise your team or manager. If the real reason is sensitive (layoff, conflict), give a brief, neutral truth.

**Trade-off.** Overly polished answers sound rehearsed; overly honest negativity sounds risky. Aim for true and constructive.

**Evidence.** Concrete steps you have already taken toward the move (projects, study, side builds).

**Failure mode to mention.** Complaining about compensation or colleagues, or contradicting what you said in your cover message.

**60-90 second version:** "I've spent [N years] building backend systems and APIs, and I've learned [specific skill]. Over the last [period] I've been building [AI project] and I want to do that work full time, which my current role doesn't offer. This role stands out because [specific reason from the JD], and my experience with [A] and [B] gives me a fast start."

**Follow-ups.** *Why this company?* One real reason tied to their product or problem. *What if we can't offer more AI work immediately?* Say what you would still gain and how you would contribute.

## Q4. Walk me through your resume / tell me about yourself.

**Define.** A two-minute narrative that links your past to this role.

**Mechanism.** Present, past, future: what you do now; two or three steps that built relevant skills; why this role is next. Keep to the positioning statement.

**Decision.** Skip unrelated details; save depth for follow-ups.

**Trade-off.** Too short leaves them guessing; too long loses them.

**Evidence.** One project or result per phase.

**Failure mode to mention.** Reading the resume aloud in order.

**60-90 second version:** "I'm a software engineer focused on backend systems and APIs. [Current role, one result]. Before that [relevant step]. Over the last year I've been moving into AI applications: I built [project], a RAG system with [features] and [evaluation], and I'm learning [next area]. I'm looking for a role where I build and operate LLM-powered products, which is why [company role] interested me."

**Follow-ups.** *Which part do you enjoy most?* A specific kind of problem. *Where do you want to be in two years?* Deeper ownership of production AI systems.

## Q5 (added). Tell me about the AI project on your resume. How do you know it works?

**Define.** A request for an evidence-based project story.

**Mechanism.** Problem, architecture in one breath, two decisions with rejected alternatives, evaluation (dataset, metric, result, limits), one failure and the fix, and what is not production-ready.

**Decision.** Lead with evaluation, because it shows engineering maturity. **Trade-off:** depth versus time; offer to expand. **Evidence:** README, eval set, commit history. **Failure mode to mention:** quoting an accuracy number with no dataset behind it.

**60-90 second version:** "It's a [type] system for [users]. Architecture: [five-word summary]. I chose [A] over [B] because [reason]. I evaluated on [N] questions I labelled myself, got [result], and the main failure was [X], which I fixed by [Y]. It's a project, not production: [limits]."

**Follow-ups.** *How was the eval set made?* Describe sources and labelling. *What would break at 100x?* Name one or two bottlenecks.

## Q6 (added). Have you used this in production?

**Define.** A direct honesty check. **Mechanism.** Answer yes or no first. If no, describe the closest real experience and exactly what you would validate. **Decision:** never stretch "production". **Trade-off:** short-term discomfort for long-term trust. **Evidence:** deployed demo, monitoring you set up, load tests. **Failure mode to mention:** being caught inflating a side project.

**60-90 second version:** "Not with real customer traffic. I deployed it on [platform] with logging, health checks and an eval gate, and load-tested it to [measured]. In production I'd additionally need on-call, SLOs and cost controls, which I've designed on paper and in a drill."

**Follow-ups.** *What would you monitor first?* Error rate, p95, token cost, quality proxies. *How would you handle an outage?* Describe the runbook.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Interview tab: a spoken-answer failure, the actual next question, and the essay you would not say out loud. The resume listed 'LangChain, LlamaIndex, RAG, agents, fine-tuning' for a weekend clone. The README was the framework's README. Target companies were a list of logos with no JD decode and no person to write to. A bullet said 'reduced latency 50%' with no before/after or workload. In the screen they could not map each claim to a file or a metric. They applied to scientist roles with no maths story.

## Interview follow-up

You already gave a 90-second answer; this is the probe. Interviewer: 'This bullet says you built a production RAG. What is in production?' Outline: who uses it, the eval that gates a release, the on-call path, and what is still a prototype. Follow-up: 'Why this company?' Answer: one product constraint from their JD (permissions, cost, language) and how your artifact speaks to it.

## What you would cut

Say less: keep define, mechanism, decision, trade-off, evidence. Cut the tool salad, the unofficial title, and any number you cannot source. Keep three evidence-backed bullets, a README that is yours, and a tracker of companies with a decoded JD.

parts.body:
## Week plan (Mar 1-7)

The playbook schedule for the week, with the resume work woven in. Each day has about 45 to 60 minutes beyond DSA.

| Day | Playbook task | Do this |
|---|---|---|
| Mon Mar 1 | Audit resume and map every claim to evidence; list target roles | Build the claims-to-evidence table; run `audit_bullet` on every bullet; write 3 to 4 role-family profiles |
| Tue Mar 2 | Python coding mock; review bugs and complexity | 45-minute timed Python problem, then write down each bug, its cause and the complexity of your final solution |
| Wed Mar 3 | SQL timed set; explain indexes and query plans | 4 SQL problems in 45 minutes; run `EXPLAIN` on two, explain index choice aloud; load `tracker.sql` and write a new query for it |
| Thu Mar 4 | LLM fundamentals oral exam | Closed-book spoken answers: tokens, attention, inference, hallucinations; record yourself and mark gaps |
| Fri Mar 5 | RAG architecture whiteboard | Draw chunking, retrieval, reranking and citations from memory; defend each choice |
| Sat Mar 6 | Full RAG mock plus project demo; score yourself | 60-90 minute mock: design questions plus a 10-minute project demo; use the 1-5 rubric |
| Sun Mar 7 | Review misses; refine resume bullets and project README | Redo misses; rewrite weak bullets; finish README sections for evaluation and failure analysis; update the tracker |

## Proof artifact: resume v1 plus target company tracker

**Done when:**
- Every resume bullet passes `audit_bullet` or has a written reason it does not.
- The claims-to-evidence table exists, including the weakest part of each claim.
- The positioning statement is edited so that every noun is true.
- At least 3 role-family profiles and 20 tracker rows exist, each with JD requirements, gaps, fit, referral and next action with a date.
- The top third is tailored for your top 3 target roles (three saved versions).
- Project README has architecture, key decisions, evaluation, failure analysis and limits.
- You can answer Q1 to Q6 aloud in 90 seconds each.

## Readiness self-score (resume and targeting)

| Score | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| 0 | Not studied |
| 1 | Recognise the terms and the structure of a good bullet |
| 2 | Resume exists but some claims lack evidence |
| 3 | Every claim is evidenced; you can answer the screens closed book |
| 4 | Tailored versions, working tracker, README with real evaluation and failures |
| 5 | Handle every follow-up, including weakness, gaps and "have you done this in production" with calm specifics |

## Worked failure

Use this on the Week plan tab: a failure in the weekly routine, a Sunday follow-up, and the work that produced no artifact. The resume listed 'LangChain, LlamaIndex, RAG, agents, fine-tuning' for a weekend clone. The README was the framework's README. Target companies were a list of logos with no JD decode and no person to write to. A bullet said 'reduced latency 50%' with no before/after or workload. In the screen they could not map each claim to a file or a metric. They applied to scientist roles with no maths story.

## Interview follow-up

Sunday: what will you actually score? Interviewer: 'This bullet says you built a production RAG. What is in production?' Outline: who uses it, the eval that gates a release, the on-call path, and what is still a prototype. Follow-up: 'Why this company?' Answer: one product constraint from their JD (permissions, cost, language) and how your artifact speaks to it.

## What you would cut

If it does not become a spoken answer, a sketch, a query, or a story, it is optional this week. Cut the tool salad, the unofficial title, and any number you cannot source. Keep three evidence-backed bullets, a README that is yours, and a tracker of companies with a decoded JD.

lessons.title: Coding and SQL mock loop: timed rounds, scorecards, error log
lessons.summary: Run timed coding, SQL and Python backend mocks with a fixed 45-minute script, score them on a 1-5 rubric, and turn every miss into a drill via an error log.
keyPoints: Run every coding round with the same script: clarify, examples, brute force, optimise, code, dry run, test, wrap up.
Token-budgeted chunking, LRU with TTL, token-bucket limiting and top-k heaps are realistic AI-engineer screens; know their complexity and edge cases.
In SQL, state the grain first, avoid join fan-out, prefer NOT EXISTS to NOT IN, and know LAG, DENSE_RANK and percentile_cont.
Backend practicals reward transient-only retries with jittered backoff, validated LLM output, bounded concurrency and injected clocks.
An error log with category, root cause, rule and spaced re-solves from a blank file beats re-reading solutions.
Score every mock on six dimensions with a line of evidence, and drill the two biggest gaps rather than adding topics.

check.q: In a 45-minute coding round, you are blank on the optimal approach at minute 8. What is the best move?
options: Keep thinking silently until the idea arrives
Code a correct brute force, state its complexity, then optimise
Ask the interviewer to give the full solution
Skip to writing tests for an imagined solution
check.why: A correct, clearly analysed brute force earns signal and often reveals the optimisation. Silence and skipping steps cost more than a slow but correct start.

check.q: Which SQL pattern is safest for 'users who never had an error' when the error column can contain NULL user ids in the subquery?
options: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM calls WHERE status = 'error')
LEFT JOIN then COUNT(*) = 0
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM calls c WHERE c.user_id = u.id AND c.status = 'error')
GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 0
check.why: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery produces a NULL, because the comparison becomes unknown. NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and states the intent directly.

check.q: Why does a token-bucket limiter cap the refilled tokens at capacity?
options: To keep arithmetic in integers
To make retry_after return zero
To avoid reading the clock twice
To stop long idle periods from creating an unbounded burst
check.why: Without the cap, a key idle for an hour would accumulate thousands of tokens and could burst far beyond the intended maximum. Capacity defines the maximum burst.

parts.body:
> **Outcome:** Two timed coding rounds, one SQL round, revisit DSA error log.
> **Prerequisites:** Python and SQL weeks; daily DSA.
> **Estimated time:** 50 min reading, then the hands-on task. Produce: Scorecards + weak-area drills.

## What this week is

Weeks 1 to 20 taught you topics. This week you stop learning and start **performing under interview conditions**: a timed coding round, a SQL round, a Python backend practical, and a review loop that turns every miss into a drill. The output is not knowledge, it is **evidence**: scorecards and a list of weak areas that you then fix.

The coding and SQL rounds in AI-engineer loops are usually not exotic. Expect the same shapes as a backend loop, dressed in LLM clothing: pack text into a token budget, cache with expiry, rate limit a provider, keep the top k of a stream, merge overlapping spans, aggregate a call log. They test whether you can think out loud, write correct code, and check it.

## The 45-minute round: a fixed structure

Most interviewers give one medium problem in about 45 minutes, sometimes two easier ones. The winning move is to **run the same script every time**, so structure costs you no thinking.

| Minutes | Phase | What you do and say |
|---|---|---|
| 0-5 | Clarify | Restate the problem. Ask about input size, types, duplicates, empty input, ordering, what to return on error. Say your assumptions aloud. |
| 5-8 | Examples | Write one normal and one edge example. Hand-trace the expected answer. This becomes your first test. |
| 8-12 | Brute force | State the simplest correct approach and its complexity. Do not code it unless the optimal idea does not come. |
| 12-17 | Optimise | Name the idea (heap, hash map, two pointers, sorting, window, token bucket). Say why it beats brute force. Get a nod before coding. |
| 17-32 | Code | Write clean code with clear names. Narrate decisions, not every keystroke. |
| 32-37 | Dry run | Trace your own example through the code line by line. Fix bugs calmly. |
| 37-43 | Edge cases and tests | Empty, single element, duplicates, boundary values, invalid input. Write 4-6 asserts. |
| 43-45 | Wrap up | State time and space complexity, and one thing you would change with more time. |

If two problems share 45 minutes, compress to about 20 each and skip the brute-force discussion when the optimal idea is obvious. If you are blank at minute 8, code the brute force, make it correct, then optimise. A correct slow answer beats a half-written clever one.

## What interviewers actually score

Interviewers fill a form after the round. Map your behaviour onto the rubric you will use all week (1 to 5 per dimension):

| Dimension | Coding-round meaning | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Problem framing | Clarifying questions, examples, restating | Starts typing immediately | Asks some questions, misses an edge | Surfaces constraints and edge cases before coding |
| Technical correctness | Code works on the tests | Does not run or wrong approach | Works on the main path | Correct including edge cases |
| Trade-offs | Complexity, alternatives, memory vs time | No complexity stated | States complexity of final code | Compares two approaches and says when each wins |
| Communication | Narration, structure, recovering from hints | Long silences | Explains when asked | Steady, structured, takes hints well |
| Testing and reliability | Dry run, asserts, invariants, error handling | No tests | Tests the happy path | Tests edges, injects clock or IO, thinks about failure |
| Ownership and evidence | Finds own bugs, reflects, follows the error log | Blames the problem | Fixes bugs when pointed out | Finds own bug, names the root cause, states the rule |

Score yourself honestly right after each mock, from a recording or notes, and write one sentence of evidence for each score. A 3 with evidence is more useful than a vague 4.

## The error log: how you improve in 7 days

Re-reading solutions feels productive and teaches little. An **error log** forces you to name why you failed and to re-attempt later.

**One row per failed or slow problem:**

| Column | Example |
|---|---|
| Date and problem | Mar 2, merge intervals variant |
| Category | misread / wrong pattern / off-by-one / missed edge case / complexity / API or syntax / communication |
| Root cause (one sentence) | I sorted by end time instead of start time |
| Rule | For interval problems, sort by start first and compare with the last merged end |
| Next reviews | +1, +3, +7, +21 days |
| Status | open / passed once / closed (passed twice, unaided) |

**Review protocol:** open a blank file, set a timer to the problem's target time, solve with no notes and no autocomplete. It passes only if it is correct, in time, and with no hint. Failing a review resets the interval.

**Weekly pattern count:** tally categories. The top two categories are your drills. If "missed edge case" is 40 percent of the log, your fix is a pre-code ritual (empty, one, duplicates, boundary), not more problems. If "wrong pattern" dominates, drill pattern recognition: read 10 problems, name the pattern and complexity for each without coding.

## The SQL round

SQL screens test whether you can reason about **grain** (what one row means) and window functions. A reliable method:

1. **State the grain** of the output: one row per user per day? per model?
2. **Sketch the output columns** before writing joins.
3. **Build in CTEs**, one idea each, so you can verify each step by eye on a tiny table.
4. **Check on a 5-row example** by hand.

Checklist of traps interviewers love:

- **Join fan-out:** joining a one-to-many then summing the one side double-counts. Aggregate first, then join.
- **NULL semantics:** `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(col)` skips NULLs; `x NOT IN (subquery)` returns nothing if the subquery contains a NULL, so prefer `NOT EXISTS`.
- **WHERE vs HAVING:** WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups.
- **Ranking:** `ROW_NUMBER` breaks ties arbitrarily, `RANK` leaves gaps, `DENSE_RANK` does not. Ask which the tie rule should be.
- **Window frames:** `ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` is by row count, not by calendar. A rolling 7-day average over data with missing days needs a date spine or a `RANGE` frame with an interval.
- **Percentiles:** `percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x)` in PostgreSQL. Averages hide tail latency, which is why LLM dashboards use p50 and p95.

## The Python backend practical

This round is a small real task, 45 to 60 minutes: call a flaky API, validate its output, process a batch, and test it. What the interviewer is checking:

- **Retries only for transient errors** (timeouts, 429, 5xx), with exponential backoff and **jitter**. Never retry a 400 or a validation failure blindly.
- **Timeouts everywhere.** A call without a timeout is a bug.
- **Validate untrusted output.** LLM output is text. Parse it, check types and ranges, and give a bounded repair attempt.
- **Bounded concurrency.** `asyncio.gather` over 10,000 items opens 10,000 connections. Use a semaphore.
- **Idempotency.** If a retry can double-charge or double-send, you need an idempotency key.
- **Testability.** Inject the clock, the sleep function and the random source so tests run in milliseconds and are deterministic.

## Common failure modes (and the cheap fix)

| Failure | Cheap fix |
|---|---|
| Typing before understanding | Force the 5-minute clarify and example phase |
| Silent for minutes | Say "I am considering X because Y" every minute or so |
| Optimising too early | Brute force first, then improve |
| Off-by-one in windows | Test the smallest input and the exact boundary |
| No tests | Reserve the last 6 minutes, write asserts before saying "done" |
| Panic after a hint | A hint is normal. Restate it, apply it, keep the structure |
| Relying on autocomplete | Practise in a plain editor, so imports and method names are yours |

## When to ask for a hint

Ask after you have tried for about 5 minutes with a stated approach and you can say precisely where you are stuck: "I have the window idea but I cannot see how to drop expired elements in O(1)." Precise questions get useful hints and signal good judgement. Asking at minute 2 with no attempt signals the opposite.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. Two timed rounds were done with the notes open and no scorecard. The SQL set was untimed. The error log had titles but no edge case or complexity. They re-solved the same easy array problem three times and skipped the graph miss. Communication score was left blank 'because it was just practice'. Week two they still jumped into code without restating the question.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer (self): 'What changed after last Saturday's 2 on framing?' Outline: you now restate, ask one clarifier, and state complexity before coding. Follow-up to yourself: 'Which error-log item is due today?' Answer with a date and the pattern, not a vibe.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut a third untimed set and any mock you do not score. Keep two timed coding rounds, one SQL, a filled rubric, and the due re-solves.

## How to use this part

Run each problem as a **real timed mock**: open a blank file, set the timer, read only the prompt, solve aloud (or record yourself), then compare with the solution below. Record a 1-5 score per rubric dimension in a scorecard. Each solution has a `test_*` function. The block of tests at the bottom is the kind you should write in the last six minutes.

Python runs all of these with the standard library only. Run a file with `python3 -c "import chunker; chunker.test_chunker()"`, or just use pytest, which collects the `test_` functions.

## Problem 1: token-budgeted chunker (target 20-25 min)

**Prompt.** Given a list of sentences, return chunks so that each chunk has at most `max_tokens` tokens. Never split a sentence unless it alone exceeds the budget. Support an `overlap_tokens` setting that repeats the tail of one chunk at the start of the next.

**Clarify.** What counts as a token (whitespace words for the interview, a real tokenizer in production)? Can a sentence exceed the budget? What is the overlap unit (whole sentences, at most N tokens)? Is empty input allowed?

**Brute force.** For every possible split point, test the budget. That is quadratic and ignores overlap.

**Optimal idea.** A single greedy pass: append units while they fit; when the next unit does not fit, emit the chunk, build the overlap by walking the finished chunk backwards while the carried tokens stay within `overlap_tokens`, then continue. The only subtlety is that the carried overlap plus the new unit must itself fit the budget, otherwise you drop overlap units from the front.

**Complexity.** One pass over the units, so O(n) token counts plus the overlap walk (at most the overlap size per chunk). Hard-splitting an oversize unit is O(w squared) if you recount the joined string each time, which is fine for sentences; mention that a real tokenizer should encode once and slice token ids.

**Discussion points.** Why overlap exists (context lost at a boundary), why you must cap it below `max_tokens` (else no progress), why sentence boundaries beat character cuts for retrieval, and why you inject the counter (word count is a proxy; models use subword tokens, so budgets must be measured with the target model's tokenizer).

**Edge cases.** Empty list, blank strings, a unit larger than the budget, overlap of zero, overlap equal to max (invalid), a unit that fits alone but not with the carried overlap.

## Problem 2: LRU cache with TTL (target 25-30 min)

**Prompt.** Implement a cache with fixed capacity, least-recently-used eviction, and a time-to-live per entry. `get` and `put` should be O(1).

**Clarify.** Is expiry checked lazily or by a background thread? Does `get` refresh recency? Does `put` of an existing key refresh the TTL? Is it thread-safe (here: no; say what you would add)? What clock (inject it)?

**Brute force.** A list of entries scanned linearly: O(n) per operation.

**Optimal idea.** A hash map for lookup plus a doubly linked list for recency, which Python's `OrderedDict` gives you with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)`. Store `(value, expires_at)`. On `get`, if now is at or past `expires_at`, delete and miss; otherwise move to the end. On `put`, insert, move to end, and evict from the front if over capacity.

**Trade-off to state.** Expiry is lazy: an expired entry can occupy a slot until it is read, evicted by LRU or purged. That keeps `get` and `put` O(1). If you need strict expiry, add a min-heap of `(expires_at, key)` and pop stale heads on each operation (O(log n)), skipping heap entries whose key was overwritten, or run `purge()` on a timer. Mention that it is a classic interview follow-up.

**Edge cases.** Capacity one, overwriting a key, `ttl` of zero or negative, expiry exactly at the boundary (use `>=` consistently and test it), time going backwards (use a monotonic clock, not wall-clock time).

**Where this shows up in GenAI work:** caching embeddings, caching validated LLM answers keyed by prompt hash, and caching tool results for a bounded time.

## Problem 3: token-bucket rate limiter (target 25 min)

**Prompt.** Limit each user to a sustained rate of R requests per second with bursts up to B. Implement `allow(key, cost=1)` that returns whether the request may proceed, and `retry_after(key)` that returns seconds to wait.

**Clarify.** Fixed window, sliding window or token bucket? (Token bucket allows bursts and is easy to reason about.) Is cost always one? (LLM limits count tokens, so cost varies.) Per user or global? Single process or distributed? (Distributed needs an atomic store such as Redis with a Lua script; say it, do not build it.)

**Brute force.** Keep a list of timestamps per key and count those in the last second: O(requests) memory and time per check.

**Optimal idea.** Store only two numbers per key: current tokens and the last update time. On each call, add `elapsed * rate` tokens, cap at capacity, then spend `cost` if enough remain. That is O(1) time and memory per key, with no timers.

**Edge cases.** First sight of a key (starts full), long idle (cap at capacity, otherwise you create an unbounded burst), `cost` larger than capacity (can never succeed, so raise), float precision (use clean numbers in tests), clock source (monotonic).

**Where this shows up:** provider limits are usually both requests per minute and tokens per minute, so you often need two buckets and spend from both. On a 429 respect the `Retry-After` header if present and add jitter.

## Warm-ups: top-k streaming and merge intervals

These two are common 10-minute screens. Know them cold.

**Top k of a stream, O(n log k) time, O(k) memory.** Keep a min-heap of size k. The smallest of the current top k sits at the root, so a new value only matters if it beats the root:

```python
import heapq

def top_k_stream(stream, k):
    heap = []
    for x in stream:
        if len(heap) < k:
            heapq.heappush(heap, x)
        elif x > heap[0]:
            heapq.heapreplace(heap, x)
    return sorted(heap, reverse=True)
```

Why not sort everything? O(n log n) time and O(n) memory, and you may not be able to hold the stream. Why not a max-heap? You would need all n items. For top k frequent words, count with a dictionary, then `heapq.nsmallest(k, items, key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))` for deterministic tie-breaking.

**Merge intervals, O(n log n).** Sort by start, then extend the last merged interval when the next one overlaps or touches (`start <= last_end`), else append. The classic bug is sorting by end or using `<` when touching intervals should merge; ask which the problem wants.

## A SQL set (target 30 min for all six)

The code block labelled SQL creates a small `llm_calls` log and answers six questions. Before reading the answers, try each yourself from the schema. All queries are PostgreSQL syntax and were run against the sample data in DuckDB, whose syntax matches PostgreSQL for these queries (re-check on a real PostgreSQL if you can); expected results for the sample are:

| Q | Task | Sample result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Per day and model: calls, tokens, error rate | 2027-03-02 small: 4 calls, 3500 tokens, 50.0 percent errors |
| 2 | p50 and p95 latency per model (successful calls) | small 700 and 970 ms; big 2300 and about 3680 ms |
| 3 | Top 2 users per team by tokens | search: user 1 (5500), user 3 (3500); support: user 4 (3000), user 5 (1000) |
| 4 | Calls that were retries within 60 s of an error | calls 3, 8, 9 |
| 5 | Users with no error ever | users 3 and 5 |
| 6 | Daily tokens with a 2-day trailing average | 4800, 7000 (5900.0), 2850 (4925.0) |

**What to say aloud for Q4:** "The grain is one row per call. I need the previous call for the same user, so LAG over a window partitioned by user and ordered by time. A retry is a call whose previous status was error and whose gap is under 60 seconds." For Q5: "NOT EXISTS rather than NOT IN, because NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery yields a NULL." For Q6: "This frame is two rows, not two calendar days. With gaps I would join to a generated date series."

**Follow-up you should be ready for:** make Q2 fast on 100 million rows. Answer: index on `(model, status)` for filtering helps little for percentiles; the real answer is pre-aggregate hourly latency histograms or use `approx` percentile sketches, partition by day, and query the rollup. Always say what you would measure first (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`).

## Practical backend exercise outline (60 min)

**Prompt.** "Write a function that answers a question with a flaky LLM client. It must return structured JSON with `answer`, `citations` and `confidence`, survive transient failures, and process a batch of questions concurrently without overloading the provider. Include tests."

Suggested time plan:

| Minutes | Step |
|---|---|
| 0-8 | Clarify: which errors are transient, max attempts, timeout, what shape the output has, concurrency limit, what happens when validation still fails after repair |
| 8-20 | `call_with_retry`: exponential backoff with full jitter, only for transient errors, injectable `sleep` and `rng` |
| 20-32 | `parse_answer`: strict validation, with errors safe to feed back to the model; `generate_validated` with one repair attempt |
| 32-42 | `run_batch`: semaphore for concurrency, preserve input order, `return_exceptions=True` so one failure does not cancel the rest |
| 42-55 | Tests: retry count, delays bounded, permanent errors not retried, invalid JSON repaired once, concurrency never exceeds the limit |
| 55-60 | Review: what to add for production (timeouts, circuit breaker, idempotency keys, logging without personal text, metrics) |

The final code block implements and tests all four pieces. Notice what it **does not** do: it does not log the prompt or the answer, it does not retry on `PermanentError`, and it never sleeps for real in tests.

## Scorecard template

Copy this for every mock, and fill it in within ten minutes of finishing:

```
Date / round / problem:
Time used (clarify | brute | optimal | code | test):
Scores 1-5, one line of evidence each:
  Problem framing:
  Technical correctness:
  Trade-offs:
  Communication:
  Testing/reliability:
  Ownership/evidence:
Top 2 gaps -> drill chosen (pattern, 3 problems, deadline):
Error-log rows added:
```

## Weak-area drills: the format

For each of your two biggest gaps, run a **25-minute drill**: pick 3 problems of the same pattern, solve each in 8 minutes with a timer, and after each write the rule you learned in one sentence. Re-test the same pattern two days later on a fresh problem. A gap is closed when you solve a new problem of that pattern unaided, in time, twice.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. Two timed rounds were done with the notes open and no scorecard. The SQL set was untimed. The error log had titles but no edge case or complexity. They re-solved the same easy array problem three times and skipped the graph miss. Communication score was left blank 'because it was just practice'. Week two they still jumped into code without restating the question.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer (self): 'What changed after last Saturday's 2 on framing?' Outline: you now restate, ask one clarifier, and state complexity before coding. Follow-up to yourself: 'Which error-log item is due today?' Answer with a date and the pattern, not a vibe.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut a third untimed set and any mock you do not score. Keep two timed coding rounds, one SQL, a filled rubric, and the due re-solves.

from typing import Callable, List

def word_count(text: str) -> int:
    # Stand-in for a real tokenizer. Inject tiktoken or a provider counter in production.
    return len(text.split())


def _hard_split(text: str, max_tokens: int, count: Callable[[str], int]) -> List[str]:
    """Split one oversize unit on word boundaries so each piece fits the budget."""
    pieces, cur = [], []
    for word in text.split():
        candidate = " ".join(cur + [word])
        if cur and count(candidate) > max_tokens:
            pieces.append(" ".join(cur))
            cur = [word]
        else:
            cur.append(word)
    if cur:
        pieces.append(" ".join(cur))
    return pieces


def chunk(units: List[str], max_tokens: int, overlap_tokens: int = 0,
          count: Callable[[str], int] = word_count) -> List[str]:
    """Greedily pack sentences/paragraphs into chunks of <= max_tokens.

    Units are never split unless one alone exceeds the budget. The tail of each
    chunk (whole units, at most overlap_tokens) is repeated at the start of the next.
    """
    if max_tokens <= 0:
        raise ValueError("max_tokens must be positive")
    if not 0 <= overlap_tokens < max_tokens:
        raise ValueError("overlap_tokens must be in [0, max_tokens)")

    pieces: List[str] = []
    for u in units:
        if not u.strip():
            continue
        if count(u) > max_tokens:
            pieces.extend(_hard_split(u, max_tokens, count))
        else:
            pieces.append(u)

    chunks: List[str] = []
    cur: List[str] = []
    cur_tokens = 0
    for p in pieces:
        n = count(p)
        if cur and cur_tokens + n > max_tokens:
            chunks.append(" ".join(cur))
            carry: List[str] = []
            t = 0
            for prev in reversed(cur):
                c = count(prev)
                if t + c > overlap_tokens:
                    break
                carry.insert(0, prev)
                t += c
            while carry and t + n > max_tokens:  # overlap must leave room for the new unit
                t -= count(carry.pop(0))
            cur, cur_tokens = carry, t
        cur.append(p)
        cur_tokens += n
    if cur:
        chunks.append(" ".join(cur))
    return chunks


def test_chunker():
    units = ["a b c", "d e", "f g h i", "j"]
    assert chunk(units, 5) == ["a b c d e", "f g h i j"]
    # overlap=2 repeats "d e" at the start of chunk 2; "f g h i" (4 tokens) is too big to repeat
    assert chunk(units, 6, overlap_tokens=2) == ["a b c d e", "d e f g h i", "j"]
    out = chunk(["one two three four five six seven"], 3)
    assert out == ["one two three", "four five six", "seven"]
    assert chunk([], 5) == [] and chunk(["", "  "], 5) == []
    for bad in [(0, 0), (5, 5), (5, -1)]:
        try:
            chunk(["x"], *bad)
            assert False, "should raise"
        except ValueError:
            pass
    # invariants on a bigger input
    sents = [f"s{i} " + "w " * (i % 7) for i in range(60)]
    res = chunk(sents, 10, overlap_tokens=3)
    assert all(word_count(c) <= 10 for c in res)
    assert res[0].startswith("s0") and res[-1].split()[-1] in ("w", "s59")
    covered = " ".join(res)
    assert all(f"s{i} " in covered + " " for i in range(60))

import time
from collections import OrderedDict
from typing import Any, Callable, Optional


class TTLCache:
    """LRU cache with per-entry time-to-live. get/put are O(1) amortised."""

    def __init__(self, capacity: int, default_ttl: float = 60.0,
                 clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic):
        if capacity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("capacity must be positive")
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.default_ttl = default_ttl
        self._clock = clock
        self._data: "OrderedDict[Any, tuple]" = OrderedDict()  # key -> (value, expires_at)

    def get(self, key: Any, default: Any = None) -> Any:
        item = self._data.get(key)
        if item is None:
            return default
        value, expires_at = item
        if self._clock() >= expires_at:  # lazy expiry on read
            del self._data[key]
            return default
        self._data.move_to_end(key)  # mark most recently used
        return value

    def put(self, key: Any, value: Any, ttl: Optional[float] = None) -> None:
        ttl = self.default_ttl if ttl is None else ttl
        if ttl <= 0:
            raise ValueError("ttl must be positive")
        self._data[key] = (value, self._clock() + ttl)
        self._data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self._data) > self.capacity:
            self._data.popitem(last=False)  # evict least recently used

    def purge(self) -> int:
        """Drop all expired entries (O(n)). Call from a timer if memory matters."""
        now = self._clock()
        dead = [k for k, (_, exp) in self._data.items() if now >= exp]
        for k in dead:
            del self._data[k]
        return len(dead)

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self._data)  # may include expired entries not yet purged


def test_ttl_cache():
    now = [0.0]
    c = TTLCache(2, default_ttl=10, clock=lambda: now[0])
    c.put("a", 1)
    c.put("b", 2)
    assert c.get("a") == 1          # a is now most recent
    c.put("c", 3)                   # evicts b (least recent)
    assert c.get("b") is None and c.get("a") == 1 and c.get("c") == 3
    now[0] = 9.9
    assert c.get("a") == 1
    now[0] = 10.0                   # expiry boundary: expired at exactly ttl
    assert c.get("a") is None
    c.put("d", 4, ttl=1)
    now[0] = 11.5
    assert c.get("d", "gone") == "gone"
    p = TTLCache(3, default_ttl=10, clock=lambda: now[0])
    p.put("x", 1, ttl=1)
    p.put("y", 2, ttl=100)
    now[0] += 5
    assert len(p) == 2 and p.purge() == 1 and len(p) == 1
    c = p
    c.put("a", 10)
    c.put("a", 11)                  # overwrite refreshes value and TTL, size unchanged
    assert c.get("a") == 11
    for bad in (0, -1):
        try:
            TTLCache(bad)
            assert False
        except ValueError:
            pass

import time
from typing import Callable, Dict, Tuple


class TokenBucket:
    """Per-key token bucket. capacity = max burst, refill_rate = tokens per second."""

    def __init__(self, capacity: float, refill_rate: float,
                 clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic):
        if capacity <= 0 or refill_rate <= 0:
            raise ValueError("capacity and refill_rate must be positive")
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.refill_rate = refill_rate
        self._clock = clock
        self._state: Dict[str, Tuple[float, float]] = {}  # key -> (tokens, last_ts)

    def _refill(self, key: str) -> float:
        now = self._clock()
        tokens, last = self._state.get(key, (self.capacity, now))
        tokens = min(self.capacity, tokens + (now - last) * self.refill_rate)
        self._state[key] = (tokens, now)
        return tokens

    def allow(self, key: str, cost: float = 1.0) -> bool:
        if cost > self.capacity:
            raise ValueError("cost exceeds capacity; request can never be allowed")
        tokens = self._refill(key)
        if tokens >= cost:
            self._state[key] = (tokens - cost, self._state[key][1])
            return True
        return False

    def retry_after(self, key: str, cost: float = 1.0) -> float:
        """Seconds until `cost` tokens are available (0 if available now)."""
        tokens = self._refill(key)
        return max(0.0, (cost - tokens) / self.refill_rate)


def test_token_bucket():
    now = [0.0]
    tb = TokenBucket(capacity=4, refill_rate=2, clock=lambda: now[0])  # 2 tokens/s
    assert [tb.allow("u1") for _ in range(5)] == [True] * 4 + [False]   # burst of 4
    assert tb.retry_after("u1") == 0.5
    now[0] = 0.5                                                         # +1 token
    assert tb.allow("u1") is True and tb.allow("u1") is False
    assert tb.allow("u2") is True                                        # keys independent
    now[0] = 100.0                                                       # long idle: capped at capacity
    assert [tb.allow("u1") for _ in range(5)] == [True] * 4 + [False]
    assert tb.allow("u3", cost=4) is True and tb.allow("u3", cost=1) is False
    try:
        tb.allow("u1", cost=5)
        assert False
    except ValueError:
        pass

-- Q1: per day and model: calls, total tokens, error rate
SELECT created_at::date AS day, model,
       COUNT(*) AS calls,
       SUM(prompt_tokens + completion_tokens) AS total_tokens,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'error') / COUNT(*), 1) AS error_pct
FROM llm_calls
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

-- Q2: p50 and p95 latency per model, successful calls only
SELECT model,
       percentile_cont(0.5)  WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) AS p50_ms,
       percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) AS p95_ms
FROM llm_calls

                            ORDER BY SUM(c.prompt_tokens + c.completion_tokens) DESC) AS rnk

import asyncio
import json
import random
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Awaitable, Callable, Dict, List


class TransientError(Exception):
    """Timeouts, 429s, 5xx: safe to retry."""


class PermanentError(Exception):
    """4xx other than 429, bad request: retrying will not help."""


async def call_with_retry(fn: Callable[[], Awaitable[Any]], attempts: int = 4,
                          base_delay: float = 0.5, max_delay: float = 8.0,
                          sleep: Callable[[float], Awaitable[None]] = asyncio.sleep,
                          rng: random.Random = random.Random()) -> Any:
    """Exponential backoff with full jitter. Only TransientError is retried."""
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            return await fn()
        except TransientError:
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise
            cap = min(max_delay, base_delay * 2 ** attempt)
            await sleep(rng.uniform(0, cap))  # full jitter avoids synchronized retry storms


@dataclass
class Answer:
    answer: str
    citations: List[str]
    confidence: float


def parse_answer(raw: str) -> Answer:
    """Validate untrusted model output. Raises ValueError with a message safe to feed back."""
    try:
        data: Dict[str, Any] = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        raise ValueError(f"not valid JSON: {e.msg}")
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        raise ValueError("expected a JSON object")
    if not isinstance(data.get("answer"), str) or not data["answer"].strip():
        raise ValueError("'answer' must be a non-empty string")
    cites = data.get("citations")
    if not isinstance(cites, list) or not all(isinstance(c, str) for c in cites):
        raise ValueError("'citations' must be a list of strings")
    conf = data.get("confidence")
    if isinstance(conf, bool) or not isinstance(conf, (int, float)) or not 0 <= conf <= 1:
        raise ValueError("'confidence' must be a number in [0, 1]")
    return Answer(data["answer"], cites, float(conf))


async def generate_validated(llm: Callable[[str], Awaitable[str]], prompt: str,
                             max_repairs: int = 1) -> Answer:
    """Call the model; if output fails validation, ask once more with the error."""
    current = prompt
    for repair in range(max_repairs + 1):
        raw = await llm(current)
        try:
            return parse_answer(raw)
        except ValueError as e:
            if repair == max_repairs:
                raise
            current = f"{prompt}\n\nYour last reply was invalid: {e}. Return only valid JSON."
    raise AssertionError("unreachable")


async def run_batch(items: List[str], worker: Callable[[str], Awaitable[Any]],
                    concurrency: int = 3) -> List[Any]:
    """Bounded concurrency. Results keep input order; one failure does not cancel the rest."""
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)

    async def one(x: str) -> Any:
        async with sem:
            return await worker(x)

    return await asyncio.gather(*(one(x) for x in items), return_exceptions=True)


def test_backend():
    # 1. retries: two transient failures then success; delays are bounded by the cap
    delays: List[float] = []
    calls = {"n": 0}

    async def flaky():
        calls["n"] += 1
        if calls["n"] < 3:
            raise TransientError("429")
        return "ok"

    async def fake_sleep(d: float):
        delays.append(d)

    assert asyncio.run(call_with_retry(flaky, sleep=fake_sleep, rng=random.Random(1))) == "ok"
    assert calls["n"] == 3 and len(delays) == 2 and delays[0] <= 0.5 and delays[1] <= 1.0

    # 2. permanent errors are not retried; exhausted retries re-raise
    async def bad():
        calls["n"] += 1
        raise PermanentError("400")

    calls["n"] = 0
    try:
        asyncio.run(call_with_retry(bad, sleep=fake_sleep))
        assert False
    except PermanentError:
        assert calls["n"] == 1

    async def always():
        raise TransientError("503")

    try:
        asyncio.run(call_with_retry(always, attempts=2, sleep=fake_sleep))
        assert False
    except TransientError:
        pass

    # 3. validation and one repair attempt
    good = '{"answer": "Refunds take 5 days.", "citations": ["doc1#3"], "confidence": 0.8}'
    assert parse_answer(good).citations == ["doc1#3"]
    for raw in ["nope", "[]", '{"answer": "", "citations": [], "confidence": 0.5}',
                '{"answer": "x", "citations": [1], "confidence": 0.5}',
                '{"answer": "x", "citations": [], "confidence": 1.5}',
                '{"answer": "x", "citations": [], "confidence": true}']:
        try:
            parse_answer(raw)
            assert False, raw
        except ValueError:
            pass
    replies = iter(["not json", good])
    prompts: List[str] = []

    async def llm(p: str) -> str:
        prompts.append(p)
        return next(replies)

    ans = asyncio.run(generate_validated(llm, "Q?"))
    assert ans.confidence == 0.8 and len(prompts) == 2 and "invalid" in prompts[1]

    # 4. bounded concurrency keeps order and isolates failures
    active = {"now": 0, "max": 0}

    async def worker(x: str) -> str:
        active["now"] += 1
        active["max"] = max(active["max"], active["now"])
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        active["now"] -= 1
        if x == "boom":
            raise RuntimeError("boom")
        return x.upper()

    res = asyncio.run(run_batch(["a", "boom", "c", "d", "e"], worker, concurrency=2))
    assert res[0] == "A" and isinstance(res[1], RuntimeError) and res[2:] == ["C", "D", "E"]
    assert active["max"] <= 2
